Mr. Speaker, I believe there is some distinct advantage in doing things this way because a member may speak on a number of items that are of concern to him, as did the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Rae) recently.
In my remarks I want to deal specifically with the prohibition against a provincial government going into the banking business. In my concluding comments yesterday I pointed out that there are times when free enterprise does not satisfy the population. I believe in free enterprise, Mr. Speaker, but if it becomes a monopoly then it is just as bad as any other type of monopoly. As an illustration of my point I used the instance of Alberta, where in the hungry thirties the insurance companies did, in reality, become a monopoly and charged prohibitive rates. At that time thousands of people could not afford to buy fire insurance on their homes. The government endeavoured to get the insurance companies to change their rates, but without success, so it went into the insurance business itself in competition with the companies. As a result, the people had free choice; they either went to the Alberta government insurance office or to one of the private companies.
The fact that the rate charged by the Alberta government was considerably lower brought thousands of applicants to its offices which did a rousing business. Within a short time the other companies found that in order to stay in business they had to lower their rates to be comparable with those charged by the government. Eventually the Alberta Insurance Office

November 13, 1980
Bank Act
became the private insurance company which is today called the Alberta General Insurance Company, a very efficient operation which does excellent business.
I used that example to show that there are times when free enterprise is not free, but becomes a monopoly. In such circumstances, I believe that a government has an obligation to ensure that there is competition. It is the life blood of a free enterprise system; without competition there certainly is no free enterprise.
We are now dealing with competition in the banking business. This is possible. I hope it will succeed because the keener the competition, the less cost to the consumer. I also believe that the credit unions, caisses populaires, the treasury branches of Alberta and probably similar institutions in other provinces, are providing competition to the banking system, even though they are not covered by the Bank Act.
I want to emphasize two points, Mr. Speaker. First of all, there are disadvantages in the Bank Act. Had the treasury branches of Alberta been covered by the Bank Act they would not have been able to provide lower interest rates during the 1978-79 and 1980 seasons to farmers, developers, producers, and builders in the province. Because they were operating under the auspices of the Alberta government, however, their rates did not increase with the Bank of Canada rates and there was no obligation for them to do so. Consequently, they provided a service to the people. That is one of the reasons that many businesses in Alberta continued to thrive whilst there were widespread bankruptcies in other provinces.
If free enterprise gets to a point that it wants to charge all the market will bear, then I think a government has a responsibility to act, whether it be in the area of banking, insurance, transportation or anything else.
I recall another instance when competition resulted in exactly what I am trying to indicate here, and that is that a provincial government should have the right to enter the banking business if it chooses.
At one time the cost of transportation between Fort McMurray and Drumheller was exorbitant. There was only one way for freight to travel, and for most passenger traffic as well, and that was by train. The rates charged by the railway company were exorbitant. In Fort McMurray, people paid four or five times more for milk, sugar and potatoes than was charged in Edmonton. As soon as the highway to Fort McMurray was completed and truckers were able to provide competition for the railway, prices came down. In other words, Mr. Speaker, the railway was charging what the market would bear, and in my view that is not an aspect of free enterprise; it is an aspect of monopoly.
The same thing happens with our banks. If banks become a monopoly, all charging the same rates and not competing with each other, it may well be that the people of a province would approach the government to establish competition in the banking business. I cannot see why a provincial government, composed of responsible people elected by the citizens of a province, should be barred from the banking business.
There is another point that I want to make, Mr. Speaker. Originally, the banking business was handed over to private entrepreneurs by government. Since that time it has prospered, and it is not difficult to understand why. Banks provide a service, but they also have some tremendous benefits not available to trust companies, credit unions or treasury branches, such as the expansion of credit. Through this expansion of credit banks have been able to make big profits. I do not think there is any dispute about that. I have argued many times that some of that expansion of credit which comes about because of the growth of business in a community and an increase in the gross national product of the country, should be plowed back into the community through low interest loans for the building of schools and hospitals. If the banks were to adopt this suggestion they would not be subject to the criticism of making tremendous amounts of money through the privilege granted them by government of expanding credit, based on certain rules. No other business has that privilege.
The treasury branches in Alberta do a great deal of business. One of the best features is that they lend out the money of depositors. When I deposit money in a treasury branch, Mr. Speaker, I sign a paper stating that they may lend my money. They make a profit on the daily operation as a result but, Mr. Speaker, they cannot make any money on the expansion of credit because that privilege is not open to them.
A previous government in Alberta applied formally for a banking charter for the simple reason that the treasury branch could then expand credit. It was held that this would be of benefit to the people because it would mean higher payments to those on welfare, higher pensions and expanded benefits for the disabled-indeed, better service all the way around beause there would be more money available. The privilege was not granted, however. I cannot see anything wrong with that, Mr. Speaker.
I should like to ask the government to reconsider the prohibition against any provincial government entering the banking business. Surely we want this country to enjoy freedom of choice. We do not want free enterprise monopolies any more than we want government or other types of monopolies. A monopoly is a monopoly, Mr. Speaker, and the only way to break one is through competition. I suggest that monopolies can occur in the banking business; they have in the past and they can in the future. Let us keep this weapon of free enterprise. Competition is the lifeblood of the free enterprise system.
I want to conclude by repeating what I said in my opening remarks, Mr. Speaker. I believe a government, whether it be federal, provincial or municipal, has a responsibility to reflect the thinking of the greatest possible number of people who elected it. If the people of a province elect a government to create a bank in competition with the banking system, and I do not mean a monopoly, surely that provincial government should have the right to do it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to take part in this phase of the debate. 1 was pleased to hear the remarks of the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor). They reinforce many of the points made in committee and recognize a very important sphere of activity.
When looking at the series of amendments today, the one which typifies this is No. 5. By including prohibition in the act, the government is having the Crown become involved in the business of banking. That was a very serious error. Also, it is inconsistent with many of the things they are doing. The resolution before us states:
Notwithstanding subsection 7(2), letters patent incorporating a bank shall not be issued
(a) to Her Majesty in right of Canada or in right of a province, to any agent or employee of Her Majesty in either such right, or to any corporation owned or controlled by Her Majesty in either such right;
Not only is this completely wrong, but it is inconsistent with the government's behaviour in many other areas. We have a very late but definite recognition of the need for a publicly owned oil corporation to explore, develop, refine and distribute petroleum. We have had some terrible experiences in this country with the private sector such as the monopoly control, seven sisters' approach in the oil industry. 1 suggest the industries which mobilize capital in this country have the same sort of concentration and control. It has worked to the disadvantage of many regions of this country.
The member from Alberta spoke with his very knowledgeable background about some of the serious problems that have occurred in that province. Until recently, the hardship in that province was extreme. The people of British Columbia have had the same experience from a very concentrated profit oriented group responsible to a small number of individuals in this country. They have not been accountable. Their goals have not been enunciated with regard to the aims and wishes of the charters that allow them to exist.
The government should not include prohibition in the act. They should leave it silent. If governments of certain provinces wish to become involved in the mobilizing of capital within their provinces, they should be allowed to do so. It will provide competition. We must recognize that in this country there is a small population and a very large area. We have the potential for tremendous economic benefits as a result of our resources and opportunities for development.
If in certain regions of this country the private sector fails, the co-operative sector has the opportunity to move in. Later I will refer to some areas where there has been a determined effort by the co-operative sector to do this. But there are areas in which the co-operative sector cannot function effectively. We must recognize that in those areas there is a very definite role for the public sector to play.
1 ask the government to reconsider this. It would be a simple matter to delete those sections and allow the act to remain silent on this. If governments in British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba or the maritimes wish to become involved in the creation of a bank or financial institution, and
Bank Act
mobilize capital to become involved in certain regional developments which would enhance the lives of their people, we must recognize that the public sector can be involved effectively and this should be allowed to occur.
I wish to give a couple of short examples where public sector activity might have been of assistance in the province of British Columbia with regard to the chartered banks. In the small community of Sayward, banking services were terminated because the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce felt it could no longer do business there. It simply moved away and left that logging community without banking service. The nearest banking service was over 60 miles away. The same situation occurred in Bella Bella, Ocean Falls and other areas. The bank said it could not make a profit in those areas and, therefore, would no longer provide the service. What happened? These people were left with the closest banking service some 350 miles away. The bank just up and left, telling a community to do the best it could.
In many of these communities there are not enough individuals to become involved in an effective co-operative scheme. We need a public sector banking system which can spread the profits. If one area is lucrative, profits can be used to provide service to people in other areas. This would be a benefit. If the capital can be mobilized and put to use in an underdeveloped area, that area will eventually develop. It will attract other individuals who will begin an enterprise, and the communities will develop and flourish.
Rather than taking the attitude of the chartered banks toward some of those communities and going to where they can make a fast buck, this is where we should be concentrating. The banks are not concerned about whether small communities along the coast or northern Vancouver Island wither and die. They still do what they want. This problem is not only in the remote rural areas. A bank close to Victoria was closed. It was a small branch serving a small community.
The public sector should be allowed to become involved in the banking industry. It could provide tremendous benefits for Canadians, especially in those regions where the traditional chartered banks have no interest and are not providing the benefits.
I wish to summarize those few remarks. First, by putting this prohibition in the legislation, the government has created a contradiction. It recognizes that this country is a mixed economy made up of the private, co-operative and public sectors. There are no other rational options because we have a small population spread over a large area. Ministers recognized that in oil and in other areas.
Second, the private sector is not the be all and end all. We have recognized the difficulties there. Certainly this House agonized over such matters as Chrysler and Massey-Ferguson. We see a withering shipbuilding industry in some areas of this country and the failure of the private sector to become involved constructively and thrive.
We must recognize there is a need for public sector involvement, not only in industry and transportation, but in the

raising of capital for projects deemed to be desirable by the people of this country.
I would like to conclude my remarks on that aspect and open up one other. This forms part of a series of amendments to this legislation. This is a very important part. I find this difficult, especially as a result of some discussion in committee where the parties over there terminated consideration by the committee. In effect they imposed closure in support of the Liberals on the committee and, I think, left many of these questions to be discussed in the House. I would like to suggest that we look not only at this one but at the process of incorporation as being very important. It is a thing we consider to be serious. The exclusion of the public sector is a very serious error, and it is an inconsistency.
I think the question of financial disclosure was not properly addressed, as well as the business of consumer protection. Our opposition to foreign banking is clearly known. As well, there are some very serious questions about the operation of Canadian banks in foreign countries. These are very serious questions.
I would suggest that one of the most serious questions is that of competition. There is a feeling that this is simply pro forma debate. I caution everyone that our members feel very seriously about this. In fact, in committee we are given to understand that this would not be just pro forma debate but, in fact, would deal with these serious questions which the committee had considered long and hard. We understood they would come to the House and there would be some movement on issues which we felt were important and which the government did not seriously oppose.
One of the key areas is the area of competition between financial institutions in Canada. The government has mentioned this. There are some improvements to be made to the co-operative sector which could be easily handled and which would strengthen the process of competition and, in that process, would give a better deal to Canadians. I would urge the government to break this wall of silence. Let us sit down and hear something from their side with respect to what can be done to ease some of these concerns so we may proceed with this debate and bring it to a conclusion.

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before us is a series of amendments dealing with the government or government agencies being involved in the business of banking. The House must appreciate that under the British North America Act the control of banking, banks, interest rates, interest and so on, are all matters of federal jurisdiction. Consequently, it is important that the federal government exercise that jurisdiction.
One of the problems we face with respect to the regulation of credit, the terms of borrowing and lending, consumer protection and the rest of it, is that the federal government over the years has not bothered legislating. Ministers have not bothered to take their responsibilities seriously under the British North America Act. Consequently, we have had credit
unions and trust companies develop to national size. They are totally free to do as they wish, and almost conduct the business of banking-indeed, they do conduct banking-without any control by the federal government. In other words, the federal government has abandoned its constitutional requirements. In the last 12 years we have seen an increase in the number of foreign banks coming into Canada and doing business in the banking field without any control by the federal government or the inspector of banks. We have seen them operating under provincial legislation as provincial financial management companies and the like. It is about time that the Government of Canada exercised the obligations and responsibilities it has under the British North America Act.
In the amendments we are discussing now the federal government is at least coming to grips with the problem. It is starting to do something. Specifically, it is prohibiting provin-cially-owned Crown corporations and provincial governments from using the device of letters patent to incorporate what amounts to a bank. In our constitution, surely the subject of banking is a matter of federal responsibility. Surely, if we are to have any separation of powers in this country it is important that this act recognizes that the provincial governments should stay out of the business of banking, regardless of whether or not they have been successful with respect to treasury board branches. They are not in that field. They have other jurisdictions to look after.
In a country there are certain responsibilities which must be handled by provincial governments, and certain responsibilities which must be handled by the federal government. In this country the federal government is responsible for banks and banking. Therefore it must be clear that provincial governments and their agencies should be excluded from banking.
If, as the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) says, there are requirements for government to get into the business of lending and advancing money for projects, plus handling credit in various parts of Canada, then there is no question that the Government of Canada has the authority to do so. But it should not have that authority in the Bank Act. This is really an act to control private corporations in banking. If the Government of Canada is to be in the banking business, then we should have an act from the minister which incorporates a special bank in the commercial lending field owned by the Government of Canada. If that is necessary, we will do it. In fact we have done it.
We have done it through the Federal Business Development Bank. We have done it with respect to financing export trade. We have done it in a number of locations, in a small way, through Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the like. These are the kinds of activities into which the government has entered. A further example of this is the financing of wheat sales through the Bank of Canada.
The job of the Government of Canada, Mr. Speaker, is to control banking and to control it properly. If there is a need for a government or government agency to go into the business of banking, then it should be a matter for the cabinet to produce legislation in order to create another banking institution. That
November 13, 1980

should not be an institution under this Bank Act. If the government were to go into the business of banking, then why should it be tied up with this legislation which is really designed for private banks?
More important, we have a number of Canadian Crown corporations which have developed the habit of expanding their jurisdictions over the past many years. As a result we have companies in the railway business that all of a sudden decide to become developers. We have companies which are in the airline business that decide to become travel agents. Corporations such as these were never designed to go into those other businesses. That was never contemplated. It is about time we prohibited those Crown corporations and agencies from expanding further. Indeed, it is important that this government introduce legislation which will control the expansion of its own Crown corporations. Thus it will have some control over where those corporations go. This act and the sections which are proposed by the government specifically prevent the Crown and Crown corporations from becoming involved. I suggest the minister consider the motion by the hon. member from Edmonton that deals with further limiting the government's ability in this area. This is set out in motions Nos. 19 and 20.
It is important we treat this act for what it is. It is an act which is to operate as a charter for those people in the private banking business. It is not an act designed to extend credit, to create more banks, or to allow other government agencies into the business of banking. If that is the intention then a separate type of statute is required. Surely, if it is the intention of the Government of Canada to go into banking in a commercial way, it has the power and authority, and properly could produce a separate charter with separate powers. Perhaps much broader powers would be needed for the creation of a Government of Canada commercial bank. At this stage I would be opposed to that type of proposal.
There is nothing to prevent the Government of Canada from setting up a bank if it wants to, but surely not under the Bank Act because the government is just passing this act to control the private banking field. Let us not have this act as enabling legislation for provincial Crown corporations to apply for letters patent and so further extend provincial jurisdiction into federal jurisdiction. One of the great problems we have in our Canada is the overlapping, duplication or triplication of governments involved in the business of other governments. I commend the attitude of the minister and the government in preventing, through their amendments or this act, provincial governments and their agencies from being involved in banking.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to be able to share some of my thinking on motion No. 5. The effect of motion No. 5 would be to delete section 8 which reads in part as follows:
Notwithstanding subsection 7(2), letters patent incorporating a bank shall not be issued
Bank Act
(a) to Her Majesty in right of Canada or in right of a province, to any agent or employee of Her Majesty in either such right, or to any corporation owned or controlled by Her Majesty in either such right;
It seems that in some very important ways the Bank Act we are being asked to approve today in 1980 is already out of date, and yet this will form the basis of our banking system for the next ten years. Indeed, if it takes as long to revise the Bank Act the next time around as it has this time, it will be more than ten years.
We feel that the Bank Act looks to the past rather than to the future. Last Friday the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Rae) put it this way:
Instead of looking forward to the problems which in a sense are simply here today in a very small and growing form and seeing where these tendencies will take us, there has been a tremendous tendency in this legislation to look at problems which grew up in the early 1970s and late 1960s and to respond immediately to those rather than to look at the broad framework for the future.
The ideological framework of the present Bank Act denies the reality of Canada. The banks have been trying to create Canada in their own image, centralized and ignoring the regions, especially the growing economic needs of western Canada. This reminds me of the way in which in an earlier generation the banking system of Canada systematically drained and bled the maritime provinces, so that the present crisis in eastern Canada is to a large extent the result of the banking system which drained these areas of the necessary capital they needed to develop themselves.
One of the basic matters which the banking system should recognize and deal with is the fact that we have a mixed economy. Perhaps one of the best testimonies to our mixed economy was given by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor), who is not what we might call a socialist. He explicitly pointed out that he was not a socialist, but in speaking yesterday he said, and I quote:
Let me give an illustration, Mr. Speaker-this is not in the banking field but it is something similar. During the depression years premiums for fire insurance on homes in Alberta became exorbitant. Hundreds of people could not take out insurance, as a result. The government of the day was not socialist but it offered to form an insurance company in competition with the other insurance companies because it thought it could be done at a reduced rate. It was done, and the Alberta Insurance Office came into being. It was swamped with hundreds of thousands of applications. It did so well that all the insurance companies had to reduce their rates in order to stay in business. It was competitive, Mr. Speaker.
I submit that that points to the reality of Canada and to the fact that we do live in a mixed economy. We do not live in an economy which in any sense corresponds to the traditional free enterprise market economy about which people sometimes like to talk. In the short time I have been a member of Parliament I have seen the government called upon to intervene and to bail out corporations which thought they could do very well on their own as long as they were making profits, but as soon as there is some difficulty they come to the government with their hands outstretched, asking for money.
Very obviously we live in a mixed economy, and the present Bank Act ignores this fact. It ignores the direction in which Canada must move and the direction in which other major industrial nations of our world have been moving, that is, not

November 13, 1980
Bank Act
just in having mixed economies but economies in which there can be public participation.
By deleting the provision which prohibits provinces or provincial corporations from incorporating or having bank charters issued to them, motion No. 5 restrains in an undue fashion the public sector. It prohibits the growth of the economies of western Canada.
A few years ago the government of British Columbia under Premier Barrett wanted to use the financial resources of the province for public goals. This provision makes that very difficult, if not impossible. It is important that the provinces have an opportunity to use their financial clout so that they can mobilize capital for regional and local goals. I pointed earlier to the fact that the present banking system is largely responsible for the draining of capital invested by the people of the maritimes, that this capital was invested in the maritimes and that it was drained off to use for resource extraction in the west. The people in the west are tired of their region being treated merely as a hinterland and they themselves as hewers of wood and drawers of water.
So I ask, why should the governments of the provinces, which are elected by the people, not have the right to be involved in the banking business to see that some of the financial institutions which operate in the provinces are serving the needs of the people of those provinces?
I urge hon. members to support this amendment. I urge that as we deal with other amendments we recognize that we have to move beyond an ideological base which is rooted in the past. We have to begin to deal with the needs of Canada as we move into the 1980s, and we have to remember that this Bank Act will be serving our needs-or not serving our needs, whichever way we choose-for the next ten or more years. I urge that we pass this amendment and not unduly restrict the provinces.

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few comments on the series of motions which has been put before us with regard to government ownership, whether it be federal or provincial, of banks as a specific form of financial institution. The hon. member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly) has just indicated that the provincial governments need a vehicle, and he has selected banks as that vehicle, for stimulating and encouraging economic development in the regions. I suggest that there is a large number of good reasons why the chartered banks should not be that vehicle and also that there are a great many other financial institutions through which the provincial governments can have the effect that is desired by the hon. member opposite.
Certainly one of the most fundamental features of chartered banks, of the banking system in Canada, is that the banking system has the ability to create money as a result of the acceptance of its liability, the demand deposit as a means of payment of debt. This is also true, frankly, of other institutions, such as credit unions, caisses populaires and certain trust companies. But the fundamental feature of a bank and of banking, the reason why it is an area of federal jurisdiction, is that the banking system can create money. As a result, the Bank of Canada was established to control the degree to which money is created by the banking system.
From the perspective of the federal government, if the federal government were to become an active participant or an owner of a chartered bank, there is clearly the possibility of a fundamental conflict of interest because it is the Bank of Canada, another federal agency, which controls the reserves made available to the chartered banking system and thereby the degree to which the chartered banking system can create money. Here we could have a federal government bank amongst private sector banks. This creates the possibility of differences of treatment arising. This bank could be subsidized. For example, it might not be covering its own costs and, as a result, there could be extremely unfair competition and the possibility of conflict of interest between the Bank of Canada and one of the chartered banks, such as a federal bank.
The second area of great concern to me is that the chartered banking system under the Canadian Constitution is a federal area of jurisdiction. I know that in other parts of this act there is a provision for provincial governments to participate in the formation of new banks under very strict limitations. The concern I have about further enlarging the possibility for participation by provincial governments in the chartered banking system is that if we were to allow, for example, a provincial government to own a chartered bank, under the assumption that that chartered bank would live by the existing rules contained in the act, we could find a difficult potential situation where a provincial government might say, "Being a provincial government ourselves, a provincial agency of the Crown, it is not possible for the federal government to regulate a provincial government, and as a result we do not have to comply with the provisions of the Bank Act because that is a federal statute and federal statutes cannot regulate provincial governments per se."
Those arguments are currently being brought out with regard to the new national energy program, with respect to agencies of provincial governments in the oil industry. The question of whether or not the federal government has the power to tax those agencies could be raised also with regard to whether or not the federal government has the power to control reserve levels, through the Bank of Canada, of chartered banks owned fully by a provincial government. That could lead to some very difficult problems with the implementation of the monetary policy in this country as well as the control of the money supply in a more specific sense.
So I can see from the questions with regard to ownership of chartered banks by the federal government that there are potential major conflict of interest problems. From the point of view of provincial governments, there are not only conflict of interest problems but there are also fundamental questions of

constitutional jurisdiction and the ability of the Bank of Canada to be able to continue to control monetary policy.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are getting to the point where some of my previous remarks bear repeating, but the question in this one is different than we have been looking at, the basic question. It was very interesting to have both government members coming on line so clearly. The arguments of the parliamentary secretary were
rather circular. I wonder whether he actually accepts them as being serious but, as we have seen, they are quite prepared to put them on the record. I hope they will consider that this is a different option and relax their very narrow ideological view that the public sector be excluded.
Basically our proposal in motion No. 7 is to delete section 35(1) which reads:
The following persons are disqualified from being directors of a bank:
And subsection (j) reads as follows:
a person who is an officer or employee of a corporation owned or controlled by
Her Majesty in the right of Canada or a province;
It is a somewhat interesting situation where the government will often go out into the private sector. Almost exclusively in many cases it will go into the private sector and sometimes the public service to recruit people who have expertise in certain areas in order to develop public corporations. Occasionally the government goes out to recruit retired politicians, as we have seen in one notable corporation, but by and large it recruits people to handle public enterprises who have skill in the area.
A very large number of corporations are owned by the government. I can point to Air Canada, which is a very successful Crown corporation, CN in some respects, and Petro-Canada which is developing and I hope one day will be a very strong leader in the field of energy development within the country. We have seen the government move into things like de Havilland, Canada Air and various other industries. Very definitely the government is involved in the public sector. There is no dispute.
Conservative members no longer sit on the Treasury benches because they failed to recognize that the country has a strong feeling about a mixed economy and successful public enterprises which represent the interests of people, that is, the interests of people generally instead of a very narrow group of people. By and large Canadians feel that a mixed economy is very valuable. The reason they do not sit there any longer is that PetroCan did them in. Their willingness to put that organization to the sword touched the people of this country. It probably took the Liberal members a long time to wake up to the reality that Petro-Canada was necessary, and on doing it, retouched the responsive chord and now recognize even more seriously that it must expand. We would make the same argument that this is also necessary in the sector of the economy where we want to mobilize capital. These projects are very important.
They have totally rejected the concept that our prime capital mobilizers is the banking industry, the concentrated, tightly-controlled mobilizers of capital. They say the public has no place. When one considers the matter, those are very strange and contradictory remarks. However, motion No. 7 allows for another option. It would allow us to have on boards of directors of banks people who are involved in a public corporation, and these people, albeit through a rather circuituous route, are accountable to the people of Canada, not merely to a small group of private shareholders whose interests can often be
November 13, 1980

totally different from the interests of the people of Canada. There is no reason for this prohibition.
Many corporations within the country have surplus funds at times, and with connections and certain expertise these surplus funds could be invested through such an organization. There are also projects which require large amounts of capital which must be raised other than through the public purse. For example, let me again refer to Petro-Canada, the nemesis, in this case, of the Tory party when it was the government. That organization will need a tremendous amount of capital at some point to undertake some of the projects which have been outlined. I presume that Petro-Canada will undertake exploration and we will see drilling rigs offshore and in the frontier areas of the country, and eventually we will see the company distributing oil and natural gas in eastern Canada.
The government intends to pay for these activities from the public purse by a tax at the gas pumps. Perhaps a more effective method would be to sit one of the directors of that corporation on the board of a bank. From this position funds could be mobilized from the private sector.
I find the placement of this prohibition in the legislation a very strange contradiction. The expertise is certainly available and the philosophy is consistent. By and large, the prohibition is rigid and ideological. Perhaps a far better approach would be to allow the legislation to remain silent, or merely delete it. If it were deleted, the banks themselves would be in a position to determine whether or not it is in the interest of the institution to be informed on what certain of our key Crown corporations, such as Air Canada, CN or Petro-Canada, are doing.
It strikes me that the clause is inconsistent with the philosophy put forward by the government. It is not required in the act because the banks in appointing directors would naturally control the appointments.
Since we are dealing with motions Nos. 7, 8 and 9 simultaneously, I will comment on all of them together, although they are slightly different in their intent. Not only do we exclude directors of Crown corporations in motion No. 7, but in motion No. 8 we disqualify any agent or employee of Her Majesty in the right of Canada or the provinces. The government's position was made quite clear that it opposes public input to the boards of directors of banks and accountability to the public for the actions of some of these institutions. Instead of opening these institutions to the public and allowing some degree of opportunity for public input, the government closes the door and says, "No, the act is fine". It feels that the inspector general can handle this matter better. Of course the inspector general reports to the minister, but the minister in any cases is not obliged to report to the House or to any other body. The supervision seems to be no more than bookkeeping as opposed to policy.
This debate allows us an opportunity to let a little more light into these areas. My party would like to see this prohibition clause deleted from 35(1 )(m), which reads:
Bank Act
The following persons are disqualified from being directors of a bank:
(m) a person who is an agent or an employee of Her Majesty in right of Canada or in right of a province.
Motion No. 9 refers to a minister of the Crown. As we proceed up the ladder from Crown corporations to agents and employees and finally to ministers of the Crown, in the final analysis motion No. 9 is consistent with the government over-all philosophy and I do not feel that I need to elaborate further.
The ultimate decision as to whether or not people in these positions could make a contribution to the board of a bank should be left to that bank, particularly with regard to the areas of Crown corporations. The government should look seriously at deleting motion No. 7, but I am pessimistic. The government does not want public sector involvement or accountability in the banking system. I am pessimistic that it will see the light, but I appeal to the government to remove that prohibition.

Mr. Speaker, I do not understand the position taken by the government. I think it will prove to be quite shortsighted in the areas of protecting the interests of consumers and, indeed, of the public interest on the boards of directors of our corporations. It is important we remember that when the government initially considered the question of who would be qualified to be a director, many concerns were expressed about our peculiarly closed banking system and its closed brotherhood of directors. We have a system of interlocking directorships between our banks and our large corporations which gives a tremendous advantage to those corporations and a lie to the notion that we have a genuinely competitive and open system. In fact it is a highly closed system.
My party has made a number of proposals to deal with the realities of the situation. First, we suggested that the governments of Canada and of the provinces should be able to create their own financial institutions and banks, if that is the area in which they would like to get involved. It was rejected by the government. On the motion about which my friend, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Skelly) has just spoken, we said, "All right, if you're not prepared to allow the federal government to form a chartered Crown bank or the provinces to form federally Crown banks or chartered banks, why don't you at least give us the ability to have appointed to the boards of directors of chartered banks people who are in a sense agents of Her Majesty?" Of course it would all depend on the decision that it is something which must be done in the public interest. The government has said, "No, we are not going to do that either".
To anticipate such a reply to the suggestions we have made, we said, "Let's restrict the ability of bank directors to sit as directors of other companies and the ability of other companies to appoint directors to the boards of chartered banks. Let us attempt to break the stranglehold which the old boy network has on our banking system." Again the government has said no to every one of those amendments. The amendments deal with very fundamental principles which attempt to

November 13, 1980
Bank Act
introduce elements of democracy into our economic and industrial system.
1 read an article the other day which was written by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) before he became Prime Minister. 1 would recommend it to the minister, to the parliamentary secretary and to others who are interested. The title of the article is "Economic Rights", and it was published in the 1962 McGill Law Journal. The article describes the failure of our economic system to introduce any elements of democracy; it gives a graphic description of the cost to the average working person of the absence of those elements of democracy. It also describes what the author called an erroneous concept of property by which absentee directors and absentee shareholders are able to withdraw capital at any time, which withdrawal would have a drastic impact on people who are affected by plant closures and lay-offs.
I find it ironic that a Bank Act produced by a government headed by the Prime Minister, the author of that article, would contain absolutely no elements of economic planning, no elements of industrial or economic democracy, and nothing to ensure any of the rights of which he spoke before becoming Prime Minister. I think it is sad that the government would have so little imagination that basically it is only prepared to say that the business of banking is to be left to the bankers-to the same economic elite that has run this country for 300 years.
Any opportunity that the people have to take greater control of their financial institutions, any opportunity introduced by our party that would provide for competition from popular institutions such as caisses populaires and credit unions, has been rejected by the government, and any opportunity to provide for the protection of the public interest because of the activities of government has been consistently rejected by this government.
This is a statement, if you like, of the extent to which the party opposite has fallen prey to the embrace of the economic elite, the embrace of the economic establishment, and the extent to which it has rejected every single progressive proposal made by this party regarding the Bank Act.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, quite frankly 1 have never heard such rhetorical garbage in my life as that just put forward by the hon. member for Broadview-Green-wood (Mr. Rae). It is absolutely the most ideological piece of information ever passed on in this House.
If the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood was interested in promoting the expansion and development of the Canadian financial system, if he was interested in promoting competition, then I think he would suggest a far different range of options than those he has proposed today. What the hon. member and his colleagues have put forward are ways in which government agencies-which some would argue are not necessarily the most representative agencies of the people from
a democratic point of view, bureaucrats-would put people on the boards of banks and thus make them much more democratically representative institutions. I hear no argument to justify this contention. To say that putting members of government agencies, bureaucrats and public servants, on the boards of banks would make them more democratically representative of people, is not necessarily true.
The reason the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood put forward this amendment in the first place, I think, is because it was necessary in conjunction with his previous series of amendments which concerned the ownership of those institutions by governments. If governments could own the institutions but were precluded from having members on the boards, then who would sit on those boards? That is what this amendment was intended to accomplish and not all the other things the hon. member put forward. In fact hon. members opposite have forgotten why they proposed the amendment.
Given that the will of the House appears to be that governments will not be allowed to own financial institutions which are called banks in this country, then there is no need to allow government agents to sit on the boards. They are not going to be able to own shares or take part in the ownership of chartered banks in Canada.
The same argument that arises with respect to potential conflict of interest in the ownership of banks by governments, arises with the placing of government agents on the boards of directors of these institutions. The conflict of interest is precisely the same.
Hon. members opposite decry what they consider to be the fact that we have no control whatsoever over the behaviour of banks in this country. That is utter nonsense, Mr. Speaker. We are now debating passage of a bill that provides massive control over chartered banks in this country.

I would suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that the real concern of this government and of this country is for the expansion, the increase in the dynamic nature of Canadian financial markets and Canadian financial institutions. This government is pursuing a course of action that will lead to the increased competition that we all want very badly.
November 13, 1980

Through the Bank Act we have provided for the entry into this country of institutions from other countries. Hon. members opposite have fought that, of course, and they will fight it again when the motions are put forward shortly. It is known, however, that these institutions will promote competition with Canadian chartered banks.
Over the last ten years we have seen the massive growth of credit unions and caisses populaires. We want to encourage that and to see it continue. There is some discussion about whether it might be appropriate to have a federal credit union act which would allow credit unions to expand beyond the borders of one province as the chartered banks may. This would expand competition.
The act provides for the chartering of banks through letters patent and makes it easier for new banks to be formed. This measure was fought by hon. members opposite but it would stimulate competition by allowing banks to be formed and to compete with the existing chartered banks' structure in a much more direct manner than has been the case in the past. The requirement in the Bank Act that chartered banks may only be formed through an act of Parliament, which in many cases has taken years, has seriously deterred the formation of new banks. That is why there is a provision to allow the creation of new banks by letters patent. This measure would increase competition but it is opposed by hon. members opposite who have absolutely no interest in competition. They want to put their fingers in everything in an attempt to exercise control from their perspective, which, in some cases and, indeed, maybe in all cases, is not necessarily in the interests of the country.
The government has made a commitment to introduce a new savings trust and loans companies act. This act would allow the Quebec Savings Banks, federally incorporated trust companies and federally incorporated loan companies a broader scope in the financial markets. It would allow them to expand and thus increase competition in the financial market. It is our perspective, and I think that of a good many members opposite, that if we can enhance competition there will be a better financial market, more competitive rates, and the best possible service to the consumer. That is how we intend to go about this, not by allowing the federal government or any government to permeate every aspect of our lives.
There are sound, logical and good long-term reasons why we do not accept these amendments, Mr. Speaker, and why this motion is not acceptable to the government.

If there ever was an interventionist in all sorts of business, it was by that minister.
As a matter of fact, at the time the New Democratic Party had more or less abdicated any role in the determination of the
Bank Act
contents of this Bank Act, and the representations with regard to the so-called consumerism and all the trappings that go with it came out of the mouth of the now Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. It is rather remarkable that he would, in any way, approve within cabinet the acceptance of the present bill. Of course we know very well what he said when he was the finance critic in opposition regarding interest rates. He said that he would resign if they were allowed to go up. Interest rates are much higher now than they were then, and he is still holding on to the reins of office. He also wanted to put representatives of consumer associations on the boards of banks, whether they were shareholders or not. In that case certain individuals would have a right somehow or other either to engage in public snooping or do what a do-gooder does.
A very interesting section concerns officers of Crown corporations as to who may or who may not be directors of banks. In subclause (j) at page 33, the subject of amendment No. 7, it is said that an officer or an employee of a Crown corporation cannot be a director. Those are clearly defined individuals. Amendment No. 8 covers a person who is an agent or an employee of Her Majesty in the right of Canada or in the right of a province. In other words, a public servant cannot be a director of a bank. In amendment No. 9 it is the minister of the Crown in either the right of Canada or the right of a province who cannot be a director of a bank.
A few moments ago we had a debate on the question of whether a provincial government or the Government of Canada could own a bank; in other words, on whether a charter could be granted to a government for the organization of a bank, and someone said no. A government is prohibited from owning any shares in an existing chartered bank, but there is an anomaly carried forward in this act. My amendments are designed to eliminate that. I do not think the government members fully understood when they said no to my amendments in the previous debate. This act does allow a government to be a participant in a new chartered bank up to the extent of owning 25 per cent. That has never been changed and it has not been eliminated. I find it very strange that the government of a province or the Government of Canada could take part in a newly chartered bank but none of its employees, none of the employees of a Crown agency or a Crown corporation, nor could a minister, represent the government on the board as representatives of those banks. I ask hon. members then who would?
I invite the parliamentary secretary to turn his attention to this particular part. Who would represent the interests of that provincial government which is entitled to invest in the incorporation of a new bank? The parliamentary secretary will remember that during the committee hearings I moved to strike that particular part out, but the government majority blindly went ahead-I say blindly-but perhaps it was blithely went ahead in the spirit that since the government has introduced this bill it is omniscient and therefore it must be right. At that time he was making loud noises about wanting to redirect the investment in his province. He did try, but with disastrous results. But on the other hand, does the government want to withdraw from the province any right of participation in the direction of the affairs of that bank? It is a cynical exercise. I think I was being far more honest myself when I just simply said, "No way." Neither will a government, provincial or federal, be entitled to own a bank or be granted a charter of incorporation, either by way of letters patent or by way of a private bill, as was attempted with the original Bank of British Columbia. No employee of a Crown corporation or public servant, whether federal or provincial, can serve as a director. In fact no provincial or federal government can buy any shares directly in any of the existing chartered banks. Nor can it nor should it be able to take any interest in a new bank.
The act now states that a provincial government can invest up to 25 per cent in a new bank, but no public servant, cabinet minister, employee of a Crown agency or corporation, can represent the bank. Who is going to represent the bank on the board of directors? Who will be the registered shareholders, nominees or agents of the bank? That is a cynical exercise. Under the act as it is going to go through, I suggest there is not one provincial government which would invest, as I said, a bent penny in any chartered bank about to be founded. I am sure there are some bank shares held by provincial government interests through pension funds, but they can have no direct influence. Nor can they invest in bank shares for purposes of conducting business activity. It is more of a passive investment for investment's sake. That is as it should be.
I do not think any pension fund should preclude its directors from making the best possible investments. In the main, bank stocks are good investments. From time to time the odd one goes for a bump and there may be some losses over a short period of time. We have seen that in the last few years. It would be more logical, and members opposite would be more honest if they supported my amendments which preclude provincial and federal governments from any interest in any chartered bank, existing or in the future. I hope the House in the majority will be persuaded to that view. I know there are some contrary views.
May I say this in passing. I recognize the views of my friend from Bow River. He is not alone in our caucus holding such views. He and I are of about the same generation. I worked in a chartered bank during the depression years. A lot of the
hard-heartedness and what have you is a lot of folklore which somehow or other has gained credence.
I worked in a branch in rural Alberta. Outside of the current and savings ledgers, the thickest one we had to look after was the ODWOs, the register for overdue debts written off. Branches were amalgamated, maybe five into one, because there had been a period of rather rapid expansion and competition among the banks in the twenties, and they were a little on the shaky side. When the depression came, it obviously restricted the activity and the cost of operating a great number of branches. There was improved communication.
In the twenties there was not one gravel road north of Edmonton. They were all dirt roads. There were not many cars and they were not that efficient. Therefore, every little hamlet had a branch of a bank or agency because the farmers' grain tickets had to be cashed. There were certain cash requirements and there were savings accounts.
After 1925, we had more cars and more gravel roads. Therefore every hamlet no longer required a branch of a bank or an agency. This was given considerable impetus in the thirties with declining business and the necessity to reduce costs. Only after World War II did we see in some towns a resurgence or re-entry of a branch of a bank. We saw more competition in the towns which for decades had only one branch. We found branches of three or four banks. Mind you, there was a greater population, more money circulating, and more business being carried on.
Some of the major chartered banks are now on to a retrenchment of branches. Some will close as many as 60 or 80 branches across the country this year. Those are decisions that are being made. In some spots it has not turned out as well as anticipated. Others are better business spots. If the government wants to get into a particular funding purpose, it can pass legislation and create an agency. What is wanted in Alberta is more of a liberalized Alberta trade corporation to help small businesses, what may be called a lender of last resort. That is where the need is.
There is a need for advising agencies. We have the Federal Business Development Bank with an advising agency. However, it charges $30 to open the file and a $7 an hour consulting fee. Some small businessmen have complained that when they went to ask for advice about their business, it cost them $100 to find that out. That is not the purpose of a publicly funded business advice agency or a lender of last resort. If there is a public social purpose to be served, it should not be on a fee basis as is done at the present time.
My view is that credit unions have developed to the point today where they have their own mortgage companies, and that is an anomaly or an anachronism. Credit unions were founded to get away from mortgage companies. But now they have their own mortgage companies and their own trust companies. They were supposed to allow the little man to wriggle out from under a trust company.
November 13, 1980

We are preventing the banks from getting into the car leasing business, yet the credit unions are forming their own car leasing companies. There are not many needs unfulfilled at the present time. There are both federal and provincial trust companies, chartered banks, and then we will have a great number of class "B" banks offering a variety of services. It seems to me that the whole spectrum is more than filled. We do not need any government-owned banks, or even banks in which governments have an interest which would allow them some direction in the operations of those banks. I would certainly hope my amendments will receive the support of the House and that they not be defeated.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I can see that the hon. member for Ottawa Centre is as confused about his remarks as I am.
As I was saying, I think there are some very important people who are involved with some of the Crown corporations, federally and provincially, who could provide meaningful input to the boards of directors of any bank within this country. I am reminded of Wilbert Hopper, who is chairman of the board of Petro-Canada. 1 think of Donald Harvie, who is the deputy chairman of Petro-Canada, and the Hon. John Aird of Petro-Canada. I believe they are people who could make meaningful contributions.
I would like to consider some of the other Crown corporations, for example, Canadian National. I see no reason why Mr. Spicer, who is the executive vice-president of CN, could not make a meaningful contribution as a director on the board of one of the banks. There are many others who could make meaningful contributions. I do not personally know any of the people I have just mentioned. But I certainly know some of the employees of Crown corporations in the province of Saskatchewan personally, and I believe they could make a very valid contribution to the board of directors of any bank.
I think of David Dombowski who was the president of the Saskatchewan Potash Corporation and who was involved with that great corporation from its conception until just a few months ago. He has now taken over the role as the president of Sask. Oil, which is a very important Crown corporation in the province of Saskatchewan.
I think these people have some real expertise and that they might look at the banking industry with a different perspective than the people who are there now, who are strictly profit motivated and who have very little consideration for service to the general public. Many of the Crown corporations fill both of those roles and have those mandates in mind. In some of the Crown corporations they are there to make a profit and, as well, they are there to see that there is some consistency of service provided to the people who have to deal with those Crown corporations. The people on the boards of directors of banks seem to be strictly profit motivated. They have little consideration for the type of service that the people of Canada have to put up with, who are the recipients of that service. I would like to deal with the hardships that many of the people suffer at the hands of the banks. An example of this is the interest rates, which in no real way are tied to the Bank of Canada. The people who serve on the boards of directors of many of the banks have never had to suffer the hardships caused by high interest rates because they are financially secure people. 1 know there are some people on the boards of directors of banks whom you could consider average, everyday individuals, but certainly the majority of the people who control the banks on the boards of directors are quite elite individuals. They have never had to borrow money from a banking institution, at least during the time that they were on the boards of directors. They have not had to meet the basic necessities of life, such as purchasing a house or buying a car or doing renovations to their homes. They do not really

November 13, 1980
appreciate the service aspect of a bank, which is to make such things as providing transportation and the purchase of a home attainable for all Canadians. As I have said, consideration of some of these things would put a different perspective on the board of directors of a bank. They could provide a very meaningful contribution.
I see the time is fast approaching when we will be taking a recess, but I would like to say that the Bank Act has been going nowhere. I think the government must make a firm stab at explaining where we are going with the Bank Act. November 30 is rapidly approaching and we are still without the changes which are needed. I think the government and the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance had better make some pretty substantive changes to the Bank Act, instead of a few comestic ones. I would like to say that it seems to be going nowhere, in our view. I think they should start listening to some of the things that the members from the opposition parties are putting forward. They should listen to the amendments that have been put forward. They should listen to the amendments that have been put forward by this party and other members in the House of Commons. In particular, they should consider the item which 1 have talked about today, that is, the deletion of the provision which prevents officers and employees of Crown corporations from holding positions on the boards of directors of banking institutions.

In a period when Canada is concerned about her national identity, one of our major cultural institutions is being eroded by budget cuts, inadequate housing and internal political struggles. The National Gallery's operational budget has been cut by some 30.7 per cent in the last two years. While we learned yesterday from the Acting Secretary of State that the gallery's acquisitions budget
November 13, 1980

has been restored, this information had not been conveyed to the gallery. The autonomy of the gallery and other national museums has become seriously eroded, leading to the resignation of the director of the National Gallery. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton):

Madam Speaker, first of all I question the data which the hon. member is using. He seems to be acquiring the magical quality of some of his colleagues, particularly the hon. member for Calgary West, of simply using figures to fit his argument. Those are not the accurate figures on the nature of youth employment in this country. As I pointed out in the House yesterday, since this time last year the government has created over 233,000 jobs in Canada. During this past decade, while the Liberals have been in office we have had the highest rate of job growth and employment of any country in the industrialized world, and it is a record we intend to keep.
We have also had to face the fact that more young people are coming into the market in Canada than in any other country. We have tried to keep pace with this influx. In particular response to the difficulties faced by young people, we introduced new programs during the spring and summer which provided opportunities in new technology so that graduates from universities and technical colleges would have an opportunity to use their skills in jobs which were applicable to their training.
We also took the basic philosophy that we had to use the resources of the government and focus those resources on areas where unemployment was most severe, areas where there was chronic high unemployment or industries were failing. We devoted our resources to the areas where the need was greatest to ensure that there were employment opportunities. We intend to keep that philosophy because we believe that the government should help those who need help the most.

subsubtopic: SPECULATION ON FLOATING MORTGAGE INTEREST RATE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance and it concerns mortgage interest rates. The minister has said on a number of occasions that he regards the high interest rates from which Canadians have been suffering-Canadians now have to pay over 15 per cent on first mortgages and 17 per cent and 18 per cent on second mortgages-to be a temporary phenomenon and that he does not anticipate having to make any changes in public policy to take account of this problem.
In light of the speculation in financial circles that in order to be able to provide five-year mortgages they will have to move to a floating mortgage system, does the minister contemplate any changes in the Interest Act which would make this possible, and is he still seriously putting forward the proposition that high mortgage rates are in fact simply a temporary phenomenon?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subtopic: HOUSING
subsubtopic: SPECULATION ON FLOATING MORTGAGE INTEREST RATE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 do not recall having made a blanket statement that the current levels of interest rates are temporary. What I have said and repeat today is that as far as interest rates are concerned we have been on a roller coaster for the past several months. We had very high rates which dropped considerably, and they have risen again. Today, for example, the auction of treasury bills showed a slight decrease in the bank rate, and maybe that trend will continue in the future; but I do not think the situation is firm enough at the present time on which to base a long-term policy. It is quite uncertain, and I think that uncertainty has been reflected over the past six months. Certainly over the period I have been Minister of Finance no one has been able to predict with any accuracy the performance in the future of interest rates. If hon. members in the New Democratic Party have a better crystal ball than others, I will be glad to use it.

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I was speaking about the amendments to the Bank Act before the noon break. I referred to my support for the amendment to delete the section restricting employees of Crown corporations from being placed on the boards of directors of banking institutions. I tried to express that these people could offer a great deal to the banking institutions of the country because of their expertise in running corporations, in some instances large ones. Not only would they be profitable enterprises, but at the same time they would have some degree of service to the public.
It made me think back to the time when I first had to acquire a mortgage for myself and my wife to take over a home. At the time of the purchase, the cost of the home was approximately $38,000 and the interest rate was locked in at 12.75 per cent over a 25-year amortization period. Over that 25 years the cost of owning that home would be well in excess of $100,000. Certainly most of the cost is eaten up by the
interest rates of the banks, and they have very little concern for the service they are actually providing.
I should like to go back further than that time, to a time when I was involved in adult education in the province of Alberta. At that time under some of the life skill programs we looked at budgeting for individuals and families and tried to get people involved in adult education to learn more about basic education and ways of living. When we talked to them about budgeting, we were talking about it over the lifetime of a person, that an average Canadian could expect to have an earning power of somewhere in the area of $200,000 to $250,000.
Since that time and over the last ten years, this has changed quite extraordinarily. For example, if one wants to buy a home today in the area of $60,000 to $80,000, by the time it is actually paid for it would amount, at today's interest rates and the way banks handle mortgages, to more than the expected earning power of individuals in 1970-71. Certainly it does not provide a very good picture for Canadian families who are looking at buying first homes, something which should be a very basic necessity of the people in our country.
It is time to make the banks more responsive to the needs of individuals and families. Not only should they be oriented toward maximizing their profits on the money of people who have savings accounts within their banks, but they should be able.to attain some level of service similar to that provided to the Canadian public by the boards of directors and employees of Crown corporations. Also I mentioned the names of individuals who could work very effectively on the boards of directors of some banking institutions.
1 think other sections should be deleted, and I support the amendment to the section which indicates that public employees cannot hold positions on the boards of directors of banks. There are some very good public employees who could provide meaningful input on the boards of directors of banks. These people have dealt with the banks and can look at them in a somewhat different perspective from the view of the usual corporate elite who control banking institutions.
Although some of the people involved on boards of directors could be considered common, average individuals, certainly the overpowering balance is not with that group. It is with a group which has not had to deal with banks in the same manner as average Canadian citizens have to deal with banking institutions. Public employees could have a meaningful input because of their training as public employees and the expertise they have acquired in working for the Government of Canada, in this instance, or for various provincial governments across the country. They could provide a scope of experience which very few people have in the private sector and in banking institutions. Their perspective is more from the point of view of the private sector; certainly that is dominant. Some input or training from the standpoint of public employees of Crown corporations could be very beneficial to the understanding of how governments operate and how organizations are structured to serve the public. This would be beneficial to our banking institutions and their boards of directors. I would not
November 13, 1980

want to see the government discriminate against these people by not allowing them to have that meaningful input.
Before my time expires, I should like to reiterate what I told government members prior to the noon break. We want to see some substantial changes in the Bank Act. We have talked about a few of those changes today and others have been talked about by members of the opposition. 1 think they are very necessary and the government will have to pull together some of these recommendations, changes and amendments to form an effective Canadian banking community to serve the people of this country in the manner to which they are entitled. The deadline is coming very close. November 30 is not that far off; we are only a few weeks away. The government must incorporate some of these very substantive changes, not just the cosmetic ones it has proposed, in order for my party and perhaps other members of the opposition to support the Bank Act as it now stands. Before we as members of Parliament can support the Bank Act, we want to feel that Canadians are receiving what is justly due them from banking institutions and be satisfied as to the level of service they should be receiving. Unless those changes are made to the Bank Act, I think November 30 will come more rapidly than even members of the government expect.
We will propose other changes and amendments-and I imagine members of the Conservative party will propose some as well-to make the Bank Act the responsive document it should be. It should serve Canadians so that they are not dealt with harshly. The people who control the banks should be average Canadian citizens who are not interested in maximizing profits alone, so that the people who are required to deal with banks can attain the necessary level of funding they require to buy homes and purchase automobiles or other forms of transportation which are so necessary to our Canadian way of life.
With those comments, I would ask the government to give very careful consideration within the next couple of weeks to some of the amendments proposed by my party to the Bank Act so that we may in good conscience consider supporting the government on this act, the reform of which we have talked about in this House for many years.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am puzzled why the government is so hesitant to support this very simple amendment, which provides that officers or officials of Crown corporations be permitted to sit on the boards of directors of banks. There are many Crown corporations in this country. Many of them were established years ago by both Liberal and Conservative governments and they are now large, successful organizations. To name a few, there is Ontario Hydro, which was established more than 50 years ago by a Conservative government and which is one of the largest, most successful organizations in this country. Then there are the telephone systems of the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. In Manitoba the publicly-owned telephone system was established by a Conservative government headed by Sir Rodmond Roblin, I believe, back in 1908. These are very efficient organizations and their senior officials are doing as effective a job for their companies and the people they serve as any private corporation.
Under the legislation as it exists today, the president of CNR, for example, could not be a director of a bank, but the president of CPR is, in fact, a director of a bank as well as a host of other companies. Mr. Sinclair, the president of CPR, is also the head of Canadian Pacific Investments, CP Air, Cominco, Canadian Marconi, MacMillan-Bloedel, Seagram Company, Sun Life, and I could go on and on. I see no reason why senior officials of Crown corporations which are playing an increasingly useful and vital role in the life of the provinces and the country as a whole should be discriminated against in a way in which the directors and senior officials of private corporations are not.
The only reason I can find is the one which we in this party know so well, that the disposition of both the Liberal party and the Conservative party is that anything which is done in the private sector is good and most things done in the public sector are bad. If the minister wishes to make the banking system work more effectively, I suggest he encourage the heads of some of the Crown corporations which I have mentioned, and many more which I have not mentioned, to participate in the activities of the banks which play such a major role in our country.
I know I speak for the members of my party when I say we have a good deal more faith in the objectivity, the unbiased approach, the goodwill and good thinking of officers of Crown corporations than we have in the officers of the privately-owned corporations who, quite properly, are more interested in protecting their interests and the interests of their shareholders. I urge the minister and the government to give serious and
